Our policy requires that any advertiser who wants to create or edit ads referencing political figures and elections must go
through the authorization process, place "Paid for by" disclaimers on ads and have these ads enter the Ad Library. This
includes any person creating, modifying, publishing or pausing electoral or political ads.

advertisements about elections or politics. These ads will be publicly available in the Ad Library for seven years.

starting or pausing ads, adjusting targeting or any other function related to ad management.

E&E's response to due-out from A/AID's 5/30 Meeting with Russian Democracy Advocates on
how USAID can help on tech sanctions that have been limiting the reach of civil society and
independent media within Russia (see SOC below).
Russian civil society and independent media continue to face significant challenges in
maintaining a presence inside Russia and reaching their target audiences. This has been
exacerbated by the decisions of private sector tech companies to either stop operating inside
Russia or deny service to Russian passport holders.
While the intent of these policies is sound, denial of service policies do not generally impact
supporters of Putin's regime, but significantly handicap those who oppose the war. All of Putin's
enablers have acquired foreign assets, accounts, and citizenships which they can use to
circumvent denials of service. It is the most politically active and vocal voices opposed to Putin
and his war that are now cut off from access to the global information space by this denial of
service.
It is critical for private companies to continue to sanction the Russian state and citizens involved
in the Russian aggression in Ukraine. However, it is also essential to US national security
interests that privately held US companies revise their approach to ensure that denial of service
policies do what they are designed to do and not the opposite. Exceptions should be made (as
they are in official US sanctions) for verified activists, journalists, CSOs, media, and others
campaigning against the war.
Key Recommendation: Tech companies implement an inclusion list for verified actors. These
lists could be private and managed in a decentralized manner through trusted third-party
implementers, which are already interlocutors with the tech companies on similar issues in
other countries. This approach would make it more difficult for the regime to block independent
information and allow pro-democracy and anti-war activists to have a competitive edge when
using technologies that are unavailable to the representatives of the authoritarian regime. E&E
can provide a list of the organizations that should be added to the inclusion list in coordination
with our partners.
Prioritized Company Recommendations:
1. YouTube:
YouTube has deactivated monetization for anyone located inside Russia and for any
views that occur inside Russia. This has removed a key revenue source for independent

publishers and at the same time made it easier for the Government of Russia to advance
its plans for a sovereign internet.
Recommendation: Online publishers should allow organizations on the inclusion list to
monetize their content inside Russia.
CSOs and independent media can't target or advertise content to audiences inside
Russia.
Recommendation: Allow organizations on the inclusion list to buy and publish ads inside
Russia and target content to users inside Russia.
2. Meta (Facebook and Instagram):
CSOs and media can't target or advertise content to audiences inside Russia. Even
though Facebook and Instagram are blocked and declared extremist, they still have large
audiences there and our partners are currently unable to take advantage of a significant
tool for exposing Russians to independent information.
Recommendation: Allow organizations on the inclusion list to buy and publish ads inside
Russia and target content to users inside Russia.
3. Google and Bing:
Websites blocked in Russia are being downgraded in search results. Search algorithms
register user behavior such as whether a user who clicked on a search result returns to
the results page (i.e. they didn't find what they were looking for). If so, the page is
considered a low quality result. If a website is blocked, then many users return to the
search results. This sends a false signal to the search engine and search algorithms
become amplifiers of censorship.
Recommendation: Search engines should warn users that websites belonging to entities
on the inclusion list may be blocked and offer recommendations for VPNs or other
circumvention technology to bypass the blocking. Search engines should not downgrade
pages belonging to entities on the inclusion list for reasons related to blocking.
4. MailChimp:
Russian civil society civil society organizations have been denied access to their existing
paid subscriptions, their newsletters, or their subscriber databases. Email is still a good
outreach method to people inside Russia.

Recommendation: Allow organizations and individuals on the inclusion list to continue
to use MailChimp's services inside Russia.
5. Sectigo:
Certificate authorities have stopped issuing SSL/TLS certificates for Russian domains.
This has increased vulnerability to hackers and other malicious actors or forced
companies and organizations to use the Russian government's certificate authority
which opens them to man-in-the-middle attacks by the Government of Russia.
Recommendation: The ban on issuing SSL/TLS certificates be lifted for organizations and
individuals on the inclusion list.
6. TechSoup:
TechSoup has suspended its program for Russia. We believe there is room for a nuanced
policy for engaging with democratic Russian civil society within similar parameters to
those currently used by our existing ENP partners.
Recommendation: TechSoup should continue to engage with organizations on the
inclusion list.

SENSITIVE BUT UNCLASSIFIED
FOR OFFICIAL GOVERNMENT USE ONLY
Summary of Conclusions
Administrator Power's Meeting with Russian Democracy Advocates
May 30, 2023
Key Takeaways
• Administrator Power: Stated that it is inspiring that the Russian democracy advocates are
speaking out. USAID has been supporting Russian exiles. Asked to hear from the democracy
advocates about where they see the biggest challenges for Putin's regime due to the war.
•
: Shared that she fled Russian in 2012 which was the year that USAID had to leave
Russia and she founded the Free Russia Foundation. The Free Russia Foundation has resources in
several European countries and provides important programs to Russian exiles across Europe.
Several countries that the Foundation does not yet work in have asked us to set up there
including Spain, France, and Poland. The Invasion of Ukraine has been a huge tragedy; please
know that there is resistance within Russia to the war. There are many protests against the war.
The Invasion has been hard on pro-democracy Russians because we have been lumped in with
Putin's regime and blamed for this war. Before the invasion pro-democracy Russians were
considered heroes by the West for opposing Putin's regime but the war has created this
narrative that "all Russians are bad." This narrative has been an issue not only because of
Ukraine but also a deep set narrative among the post-Soviet Eastern European countries.
Messaging support from the USG on differentiating the Russian people and Putin's regime would
be very helpful.
•
: Because of sanctions Russian exiles have not been able to access banks, news
subscriptions, and some government and private sector services. Sanctions are affecting the
pro-democracy Russian exiles more than those who are a part of Putin's regime because they are
of higher means and often have dual citizenship. The sanctions have made life for exiles hard in
Europe so they either have to face challenges in Europe or risk the dangers of going to Central
Asian countries where the Government of the Russian Federation (GoRF) influence is high.
• Administrator Power: Asked what more the USG can do to support pro-democracy Russians,
including those in exile.
•
: It is important that the USG supports pro-democracy Russian exiles very vocally
and loudly. The Free Russia Foundation could be reaching more exiles as well as get information
to those inside Russia virtually if not for tech sanctions.
•
: Russian society is very isolated from free speech and democratic
expression, they don't have the freedom to voice their opinions safely. Thus, it is hard to say
whether Russians are truly indifferent to democracy or if they are just scared to express an
opinion about it. Over 20,000 people were arbitrarily detained including minors in recent years.
This shows there are many people that are against the regime and speaking out about it.

• Administrator Power: Asked about the conditions that
husband is facing while
detained.
•
: The conditions in Russian prisons aren't good to begin with even for
healthy people. Stated that her husband has health conditions as a result of him surviving
several poisonings. It is good that the U.S. supported the Magnitsky Act - all those responsible
for committing human rights violations should be held responsible not the whole country - but
need this to be enforced more. As long as Russia is an authoritarian regime it will be a threat to
the world. Russia was placed second in Virtual Private Network (VPN) services downloaded last
year. This shows that there are a lot of people in Russia who are trying to access independent
objective information. Need to support journalists and access to VPN services.
•
: For the Free Russia Foundation to do more work fighting misinformation in Russia
we need support on lifting tech sanctions against us.
•
: There are grassroot initiatives in Russia and people are protesting. We need
to support them by providing legal representation for them when the GoRF comes for them.
• AA/E&E McKee: USAID does support Russian exiles with legal representation but the program
should be expanded.
•
: These lawyers are also coming under a lot of pressure and need support.
They are often the only point of contact between a defendant and their family as well as the
person documenting all the rights violations that are occurring.
•
: Many of the Russians in exile could be the best advocates and change makers but
they need to be professionalized.
•
: Europe receives most Russian exiles but there has not been a concerted effort in
Europe to support them. U.S. support on this issue has inspired some action from Europeans but
not enough. We need the U.S. to continue being vocal about their support and to encourage
Europeans to do so.
• Administrator Power: It would be helpful in bolstering Congressional and US public
understanding of the activists' efforts if the Free Russia Foundation could share evidence for the
under-the-radar opposition to the war occurring within Russia, such as the arbitrary detentions
and VPN usage numbers.
Asks/Tasks
• Johnny Walsh/DDI to follow up with the Free Russian Foundation on how USAID can help on tech
sanctions that have been limiting their reach within Russia.

Dear Sandy,
I am writing to follow up on Mileydi's May 1 email regarding RightsCon. As you may be
aware, there will be a robust USG delegation at RightsCon with various events in the
planning stages. In collaboration with the State Department, we in USAID's Latin America
and Caribbean Bureau are organizing a Monday, June 5 event (approximately 9 AM to
1PM) focused on addressing digital repression/promoting digital democracy in Central
America (see description below). This will occur under the broader umbrella of the
interagency Voices initiative focused on protecting, defending, and promoting civic space
in Central America.
The event will include representatives from civil society organizations, independent
media, the private sector, and donors and largely conducted in Spanish. We are currently
finalizing the invitation list, as well as identifying possible panelists. We would be pleased
if one or more representatives from Meta were available to attend (depending upon final
head counts). Moreover, as we work to identify panelists, would there be interest in
someone from Meta possibly serving in that capacity? We welcome your suggestions on
both participants and potential panelists.
We are currently envisioning one panel that includes civil society and media
representatives from the region and another that encompasses donor and private sector
representatives, with no formal decision made as to their compositions yet.
Please let us know if you have any questions and thanks for your consideration.
Best regards,
Cara
Under the U.S. government's interagency Voices initiative to protect, defend and promote
civic space in Central America, USAID and the State Department will hold a June 5
closed-door side event at the RightsCon Summit in Costa Rica. We will take advantage
of the Summit's focus on human rights in the digital age to gather representatives from
civil society organizations, independent media, donors, and the private sector to
understand the challenges, identify gaps and coordinate responses for the promotion of
digital democracy in Central America. This closed-door consultation will center on the
tactics of digital authoritarianism and repression. This includes online surveillance and
censorship; social manipulation and disinformation; internet restrictions; and the targeted
persecution of independent media, human rights defenders, and other advocates and
activists. By bringing together diverse stakeholders, this conversation aims to highlight
local and regional impacts and responses; share lessons learned between sectors and
countries; identify immediate and longer-term priorities, and further coordination and
collaboration for countering digital authoritarianism in the region.

• How does YouTube decide which events require additional resources and/or focus?

understand and respond to threats, inform YouTube resource decisions
• YouTube had a proactive and thorough approach in Brazil but still couldn't predict the
level of violence
• YouTube has a Major Event Policy - Holocaust, Ukraine, mass/school shootings, etc. -
allows YouTube to remove content that claims the event didn't happen
• Working together the Community Guidelines are flexible enough to respond to
unexpected events
• How quickly can YouTube respond when there are unexpected events?

• On misinformation, there is a Hit Pause Policy - train users on what misinformation is
and how users can respond
• YouTube has Trusted Flaggers - civil society organizations - to help them detect events
quickly, plan in advance, and respond as quick as possible
• What is the process by which YouTube shares threat / intel analysis between platforms? How
can USG align with those efforts?
• Among the industry, there's a lot of sharing between Trust and Safety Teams and the
more centralized Intel Team, Threat Analysis Groups, etc.
• GIFCT is a good example of a consortium that helps to bring together industry partners
to prevent violent extremism / live-streaming of violence
More than 99% of violating / violent content is removed before there are 10 views, but
they are still trying to get better
• YouTube is working on "age-gating" to prevent certain users (under 18 yo) from viewing
violent content
• But, HR defenders will push back because of this is documenting HR violations -
need to make nuanced determinations and responses on violent content

• Constantly looking for new sources of information to inform their local Trust and Safety
Teams

and cover Asia Pacific - welcome a follow-up conversation
• Work through Ria / Josh (as "traffic cops") to set-up a deeper dive on both Burma and
Bangladesh
• Would it be helpful to have these conversations more broadly, e.g. with other industry partners?
• More regular touchpoints would be useful - build off initial GEC engagements as a
starting point - good model because it's a regular / standing meeting

industry platforms, esp. open source intelligence
• But, it would also be useful to have product / solution-specific conversations by platform
(e.g. concerns related to specific channel / video features, go to YouTube directly)
• Open lines of communication can be just as important or even more important than
resources during times of crisis
• What has YouTube learned about how to detect problematic content over video?
• YouTube is detecting some patterns in video content related to hate speech - uses not
just text, also image detection
• YouTube has a policy related to violent imagery - to detect violent videos that are also
silent
• Age-gating is also used - leaving violent content in a news report as an example but
making it limited by age. We get criticized for leaving this content and for taking down
this content. But it is a way to protect youth, without removing content.

• It's useful for YouTube to have concrete examples (e.g. channels / content) of what State / USAID
finds most problematic, especially from the Field
• For example, YouTube will get examples of VE content from NCTC and will respond to it -
need to be careful this is not construed as USG-requested content removal
• Note: State will look at building out best practices / lessons learned when it comes to engaging
technology companies on these issues. Looking to set up a process for communication,
especially in a crisis situation.

to think about how to do this and highlighted that would be good to have these lines of
communication specific to YouTube as they are a unique platform

SECOND SUMMIT FOR DEMOCRACY (S4D2) SOCIAL MEDIA CALL TO ACTION INFLUENCER CAMPAIGN

1. This is a unique opportunity to get involved in outreach for the second Summit for Democracy (S4D2).
See paragraph 2 and 8.
2. ACTION REQUEST: From now through March 28, Missions and partners willing to participate can contact
individuals who have established and prominent social media platforms to join this effort by filming a short
(15 second-60 second) video/s with their own equipment (i.e. Smartphone), employing
pictures/images/illustrations or writing their story and sharing it via their own personal and/or professional
social media accounts on Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter using the hashtag #SummitForDemocracy.
Missions should arrive at some neutral criteria for determining which influencers to invite and should cast a
wide net for non-U.S. persons in their area/location.
3. BACKGROUND: In order to promotethe messaging and goals of the S4D2, from March 29-30, 2023, the
United States Agency of International Development (USAID) and the Department of State are collaborating
on a Social Media Influencer Outreach effort; inviting participation from influencers such as regional
activists, media figures, and cultural icons from participant and co-host countries. Missions and partners are
requested to contact and invite influencers or key groups where they have an established relationship.
These individuals should have established social media accounts (Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram) and a
substantive online presence; and will post video messages on their own personal and professional social
media accounts to potentially be amplified on U.S. government and Summit platforms. Missions must
inform influencers that their content may be amplified on USAID official social media accounts. If content is
amplified by USG platforms the Mission or USAID Washington will conduct due diligence (e.g., Google
search and review on influencer posts on common platforms such as Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram).
The purpose of the campaign is to humanize the positive impact of democracy and anti-corruption work
and provide a local perspective to broader policy conversations. This message provides background and
resources for Missions and partners who want to engage their local influencers in the lead up to the S4D2.
4. INFLUENCERS: Potential influencers (from outside the U.S.) include the following, among others as
relevant:
• Emerging youth leaders
• Civil society actors
• Anti-corruption activists
• Human rights defenders
• Journalists
The following potential influencers should be invited based on their advocacy within the S4D2 themes:
• Musicians
• Theater, television, and film actors/actresses
• Poets
5. KEY THEMES: Key influencers are invited to share their story in response to prompts that will highlight
the following key S4D2 themes in their video/s on their platforms: 1) the ways in which freedom powers
democracies that are rising to the moment to solve the world's most pressing challenges; and 2) the themes
of the U.S. Presidential Initiative for Democratic Renewal, which include:

• Supporting Democratic Reformers
• Strengthening Free and Independent Media
• Transforming the Fight Against Corruption
• Defending Free and Fair Elections and Political Processes
•Advancing Technology for Democracy
6. KEY DATES: Missions and partners are requested to provide invited influencers with the following
relevant international key dates identified below for influencer content and action.
• March 27: Partner's Day (led by civil society organizations).
• March 28: S4D2 - Day Zero (thematic sessions).
• March 29: First day of the S4D2 (virtual plenary sessions).
• March 30: Second day of the S4D2 (co-host led sessions).
7. POINTS OF CONTACT: Missions and partners should contact the S4D Executive Team
([contact omitted]) with any questions or concerns related to this request.
8. REPORTING: If Missions or partners note significant response to some of these posts (post/tweets go
viral or attract a significant amount of attention in the press) please report on the influencer effort by March
25 to the USAID Summit for Democracy core team ([contact omitted]). USAID greatly appreciates
Missions assistance in this matter.
9. INFLUENCER MESSAGE: USAID Call to Action Influencer Message (for USAID Missions and partners to
encourage participation) - see attached.

(PPO), JD Maddox (TE), Alexis Frisbie (TE)

• Shane Huntley, Director of Threat Analysis Group (TAG)
• Connie LaRossa, Google Senior Manager, Gov Affairs & Public Policy

• Josh Blumenfeld, YouTube Manager, Gov Affairs & Public Policy
• Ria Strasser-Galvis, Foreign Policy Partnerships Lead
• Michael Maffei, Senior Security Counsel
Background:
• (SBU) Alphabet Briefed Department Stakeholders on Election Protection Lessons
Learned and Global Election Priorities for 2023 and 2024: On December 7,
Alphabet's Vice President of Trust & Safety Laurie Richardson and Threat Analysis
Group Director Shane Huntley briefed Department seniors and expert level
representatives from GEC, CDP, DRL, INR, WHA, EUR, NEA, AF, SCA, EAP, CT, as
well as USAID, and DHS. Alphabet separately briefed DNI's FMIC in a 12/7 discussion.
In addition, Alphabet holds regular meetings with other platforms to share
information/concerns.
SENSITIVE BUIT UINCLASSIFIED

Key Takeaways:
General Background on Trust& Satety,Threat Analysis Group (TAG) and 2022 Elections
• (SBU) Alphabet stated 2016 was an inflection point, with a post-election drive of forensic
review occurring among many platforms. A narrower set of actors (such as Russia's
Internet Research Agency - IRA) were the focus.
• (SBU) Alphabet emphasized they saw fewer threats (focusing on foreign only) than
expected during the 2022 U.S. and Brazil elections but noted there is a much more
complex landscape of actors and information ecosystem health at play. This has made
comprehensive policies and new tools/levers to address mis/disinformation important.
Gray area speech, which can ultimately be harmful, is very difficult to address with
specific policies, however, making authoritative voices and content critical.
• (SBU) Alphabet focused on potential threats to election workers and established
the ability for persons (in certain regions) to remove PIl from Google Search.
They noted this PIl removal is a new and important effort that they want to
continue to expand.
• (SBU) TAG noted threat actors like Russia and PRC did not appear particularly focused
on the US; most of what Alphabet saw were narratives that were tangentially related to
other ongoing crises (like Ukraine) and linked to videos already published
• (SBU) Alphabet complements its policy and authoritative content work with Google's
TAG, which works to understand and counter serious abuses to its platforms. There are
around 270 cyber threat actors, globally, and three buckets of categories that TAG
focuses on: government backed threat actors, cyber threats, and global non-governmental
threat actors (e.g., Dragonbridge - linked to China, though not directly to the PRC).
• (U) External information source: Google Threat Analytics Group (TAG) noted in
its Q4 report that they "terminated 76 YouTube channels as part of [an]
investigation into coordinated influence operations linked to Brazil. The campaign
was sharing content in Brazilian Portuguese that was supportive of Brazilian
President Jair Bolsonaro." (TAG Blog)
• (U) External information source: Mandiant (acquired by Alphabet in 2022) "said
a threat group known as Dragonbridge [attempted] to sway Americans to not vote
during the upcoming election through fake social media accounts and falsified
news articles. In its campaign, Dragonbridge..spread false narratives that a well-known
hacking group based in China is actually a U.S. government group, and it claimed that the
U.S. was responsible for the Nord Stream gas pipeline explosions." (Axios)
• (SBU) Since crafting policies to address gray-area language are very difficult, TAG's
work to trace threat signatures or themes to specific content/actors can be shared
with Trust & Safety for review and action. This helps Alphabet refrain from having to
review each video; clips where the content may fall in a gray-zone, but the signature is
linked to threat actors, is critical to scaling and addressing possible platform abuses.
SENSITIVE BUȚ UNCLASSIFIED

Broad Lessons Learned & Prep for Elections 2023, 2024
• (SBU) Alphabet underscored the role and importance of authoritative content in
protecting global elections and information consumers in general. In general, third
parties that can support and corroborate results or information are critical to
Alphabet's Trust & Safety infrastructure.
• (SBU) Alphabet noted it wants to increase its automated solutions, including languages,
to scale response to disinformation and amplify authoritative content. Alphabet stated
Spanish language disinformation was a large and growing issue.
• (SBU) Alphabet is prepping for 2023 and 2024 by looking at what opportunities and
tools are available for threat actors to leverage/apply. Alphabet will watch threat
actors closely to identify inauthentic trends. In 2020, for example, a group of Iranian
threat actors pretended to be a specific fringe U.S. group and pushed disinformation
content. Overall, however, Alphabet is seeing fewer clear lines of distinction; lines are
blurring between hacktivists and patriots, for example.
• (SBU) Priority countries for of focus for Alphabet in 2023 include Argentina,
Nigeria, and Poland. Part of the concern includes the view that these elections are
where tactics, techniques, and procedures will be tested for major 2024 elections.
• (SBU) Priority countries/regions of focus for Alphabet in 2024 include the U.S.,
European Parliament, and India. Alphabet is already in preparation mode for these
elections. Once concern focuses on themes that might prohibit the ability to share
authoritative information (e.g. if the Associated Press was unable to call an election how
can that information be validated?).
• (SBU) Alphabet noted it has conversations with other platforms regularly and integrates
certain company/websites' information to update Google Search. When sites are not
updated, Google will review and consider the appropriateness of its inclusion in the
process. When asked about Twitter, specifically, Google stated they are working
through what is actually happening vs. the noise. From their view, the product still
seems to be working. If Twitter takes internal moderation and reviews a "different
way" for elections, there may be consideration to revisit Twitter's inclusion in the
Google search "carousel" updating process.
• (SBU) GEC noted to the group that Google's priority language capabilities may not
include some linguistic groups that are particularly vulnerable to disinformation. When
asked whether Alphabet would consider expansion into additional languages,
perhaps through cooperative programming, company reps responded affirmatively
that they would be open to cooperation on the development of additional language
capabilities.
SENSITIVE BUȚ UNCLASSIFIED

Future Considerations
• (SBU) All parties agreed that resiliency building - media literacy tools and
information ecosystem health over all - is essential. Inquiries by USAID and State on
resilience-building partnership opportunities with Alphabet were raised, with company
reps concurring that this would be a great space to explore further partnership
discussion. Google underscored that the creation of authoritative content (e.g. public
service announcements) is critical and that democracies shouldn't underestimate how
much a population can change over generations; resiliency isn't a guarantee.
• (SBU) Alphabet noted people adapt to media over time and recognizing who is
adapting where is key information. For example, Google's Jigsaw research arm
found younger generations are more likely to read the comment sections and was
being used as a tool for additional information.
• (SBU) To address disinformation or potentially harmful content before it goes viral,
Google stated AI/machine-learning, policies, and consensus were important.
GEC Next Steps/Actions
• (SBU) Following the meeting, Alphabet stated the importance of these conversations
with seniors included, noting in an aside to GEC that such an event held with Seniors
quarterly would be great. GEC will coordinate with Alphabet POC's and department
stakeholders to get a plan of action in place.
• (SBU) Alphabet also suggested to GEC a red teaming/threat ideation/hackathon
collaboration between State, USAID, and Alphabet. GEC will work with contacts and
Departments to organize.
SENSITIVE BUȚ UNCLASSIFIED

Dear Khaled,
Apologies for the delay sharing with you info about the organizations from which OTl's proposed training participants

interrupting work flow.
Our Sudan partners would like to attend Facebook web-based trainings in fact checking and mis and disinformation,
ideally as separate training topics, but they could be done in one session, depending on Facebook's prepared
materials. Our Sudan team would like two of our local staff to attend, as well as 22 representatives from the from the
following organizations:
1. Al-Harisat (meaning "The Female Guards"), is an initiative founded by a group of women and activists in
December 2019 to expand women's participation in the movement for freedom, peace, and justice. The
organization has participated in organizing demonstrations, vigils, and creative activities as part of the
ongoing pro-democracy movement, and contributed to mitigating the psychological and physical effects of
male and female survivors.
1. ATYAF Productions (ATYAF) is a youth-founded Sudanese platform and production house for
documentaries and short films focused on the Sudanese political evolution and social and cultural events.
ATYAF works in all phases of production, from ideation and concept design to production, shooting, and
editing. ATYAF's focus is on producing character-driven documentary films (short and feature-length) around
true stories and real issues, and engaging activists, organizations, and the public in telling their stories
through films that translate complicated, layered ideas into audio-visual forms that are accessible and
consumable by the general public.
1. Beam Reports is a data-driven and citizen-centric web-based explanatory news company that works on
empowering the public with trustworthy explanatory news to increase citizen participation and counter
disinformation and misinformation. Beam Reports' mandate is to provide a platform that will support
democratic actors to communicate more freely and securely and empower Sudanese citizens with accurate
information to actively participate in their communities. Beam Reports core work is not only reporting on
news, but also explaining the news in a way that is simplified, based on research, and produced using
creative visuals.

1. Sudanese Center for Media and Information Literacy (SCMIL) is a media center that works in spreading
concepts, skills, and building a culture of positive interaction with media tools and communication technology
tools. SCMIL works with both traditional and social media to reduce their negative impacts, is contributing to
the promotion of UNESCO's media and information literacy objectives, works on improving access to
information and media content, and facilitates critical evaluation and use of media. The Center focuses also
on countering disinformation and promoting peaceful coexistence.
1. Radio Banat FM 92.6 is the first and only radio station in Sudan specialized in and focused on women's and
gender issues. OTI is providing support for an 18-day comprehensive training camp for young female
journalists aimed at increasing women's representation, engagement, and visibility of women in the media
sector to promote media gender equality and counter gender stereotypes.
1. NUAAR is an independent media development and production company that creates safe spaces for the
expression of diverse and alternative voices; mobilizing a sense of community for women, youth and
minorities from all walks of Sudanese life by providing media content that uses participatory communication to
capture the complexity of people in Sudan. OTIis partnering with NUUAR to produce the female led talk
show, Baranda, which uses an edutainment approach to talk through women's role and interest in the political
transition.
1. Resistance Committees (RCs) are grassroots, neighborhood level political organizations that initially
emerged in Sudan in 2012 when grassroots youth networks began to collectively organize against the Bashir
